books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence
Madison's Presidency and the War of 1812

stimulus.text:
Henry Clay, a congressman from Kentucky, spoke in the House of Representatives on January 22, 1812, urging the United States to build up its navy:

“Sir, if you wish to avoid foreign commerce; give up all your prosperity. It is the thing protected, not the instrument of protection, that involves you in war. Commerce engenders collision, collision war, and war, the argument supposes, leads to despotism. Would the councils of that statesman be deemed who would recommend that the nation should be unarmed—that in the art of war, the material spirit, and martial exercises, should be prohibited—and that the great body of the people should be taught that the national happiness was to be found in perpetual peace alone? No, sir.”
stimulus.source_note: Henry Clay, Speech on the Increase of the Navy, House of Representatives, January 22, 1812; wording verified against Wikiquote's sourced text. Public domain.

options.misconception: Federalists opposed the war; Clay pushed for it.
Those were New England Federalists who opposed the war.
That was an earlier New England Federalist group, against the Louisiana Purchase.

rationales.A: The Federalists opposed war with Britain because it wrecked their trade. Clay was on the other side, pressing for war.
rationales.B: Clay of Kentucky and John C. Calhoun of South Carolina led the War Hawks, the young southern and western congressmen who wanted war with Britain.
rationales.C: The Hartford Convention met in 1814, two years later, and its delegates were New England Federalists protesting the war Clay wanted.
rationales.D: The Essex Junto was a group of New England Federalists who opposed the Louisiana Purchase around 1803, not Clay's war party of 1812.
rationales.general:
1. Place the speaker. Clay is urging Congress to build a navy and accept the risk of war.
2. Ask who wanted war in 1812. The young southern and western congressmen, called War Hawks, did.
3. Put it together. Clay led that group, with John C. Calhoun of South Carolina beside him.
Background: The War Hawks also wanted Canada and Florida, and they blamed Britain for arming Native peoples in the West.
Remember: when a speaker urges war, ask which group in Congress was already urging the same thing.
